Vice President JD Vance has whipsawed between three different roles in the past few weeks, in part pushed and pulled by President Trump himself.

   Initially, it looked like Vance was going to be negotiating with Iranians on how to end the war.

   Trump cancelled that plan and said he wanted Vance focused on rooting out fraud in Democratic-run states.

   Then, right before he was to speak at a New York Times event, Vance took on the government’s response to a series of tech outages that had conspiracy theories flying.

   The morning after the midterm elections, Vance wrote a lengthy post on X saying the heavy GOP losses were due to one reason: the Iran War. Some read this as an implicit critique of Trump, his boss, though Vance didn’t explicitly connect those dots. Vance also didn’t say in the post that going to war with Iran was the right decision.

   Interviewed in China, Trump was asked by Fox News why Vance was pulled out of the Iran talks. He said the vice president was doing a “very good job” but immediately mentioned Vance’s post (he wasn’t asked about it).

   “He basically just left one thing out,” Trump said. “ ‘If we had it to do again, would you do it again?’ And the answer is ‘absolutely yes.’ ”

   The dynamic between Trump and Vance will be very closely studied. Will Trump back him if Vance runs in 2028? The answer, as of now, doesn’t appear to be “definitely.”

   In an October interview with Mark Halperin, Vance said he thought Trump would endorse him if he ran for president. Trump was asked about this and said the two had never discussed the matter. He declined to say if he’d support him over others.

   Rob Bonta: California’s attorney general has issued an investigative subpoena to Nvidia, opening a probe into the conduct of the chip maker.

   Trump’s Friday: The president has a policy meeting this morning and will hold a news conference at 12 p.m. ET. He will then host a reception at 3:30 p.m.

SCOTT APPLEWHITE/AP   Republicans are more willing to block Trump’s nominees. A series of Trump picks have run into trouble in the past week, with a Government Accountability Office nominee getting some tough questions on Thursday after the FDA selection was pulled days ago. It shows that Republicans in this lame duck Congress are less willing to hold their noses and back nominees as they head into the minority.

   The   Pentagon is struggling to shore up GOP support for a record-setting budget. The effort to push through a $1.5 trillion spending request has stalled, as several GOP members balked at the idea of passing $350 billion of it through reconciliation. The uncertainty comes as the government barrels toward a Dec. 11 deadline, after which funding for the federal government will lapse.

   The U.S. has floated the idea of NATO membership for Ukraine in recent talks . In closed-door peace talks over the past few months, Trump’s son-in-law and special envoy Jared Kushner has discussed an idea once believed to be dead-on-arrival: NATO membership for Ukraine if it cedes territory to Russia. A U.S. official said negotiators are discussing many ideas, but both Ukraine and Russia would need to agree to any final deal.

       What Else Is Happening   • The Senate passed a bipartisan bill designed to speed up energy, mining and other infrastructure projects, overcoming concerns by many Democrats that it would weaken environmental protection laws .

   • The Federal Reserve board approved a smaller budget for pay increases at its 12 regional banks, with employees at the banks being told to expect 1% annual raises, down from 3% this year.

   • Russian President Vladimir Putin scored a significant public relations coup in China this week, five years after launching an invasion of Ukraine that cast him as an pariah.

   • New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani signed a horse-drawn carriage ban into law, ending a Central Park fixture that has been around for more than 160 years.

Trump Says Vance Erred in Critique of Iran War as Questions Swirl About VP
 
Plus, some Senate Republicans turn on Trump’s nominees, and the Pentagon is struggling to win support in Congress for its record-setting budget
 
 
ANDREW HARNIK/GETTY IMAGES
 

Good morning. Vice President JD Vance has whipsawed between three different roles in the past few weeks, in part pushed and pulled by President Trump himself.

 

Initially, it looked like Vance was going to be negotiating with Iranians on how to end the war.

 

Trump cancelled that plan and said he wanted Vance focused on rooting out fraud in Democratic-run states.

 

Then, right before he was to speak at a New York Times event, Vance took on the government’s response to a series of tech outages that had conspiracy theories flying.

 

The morning after the midterm elections, Vance wrote a lengthy post on X saying the heavy GOP losses were due to one reason: the Iran War. Some read this as an implicit critique of Trump, his boss, though Vance didn’t explicitly connect those dots. Vance also didn’t say in the post that going to war with Iran was the right decision.

 

Interviewed in China, Trump was asked by Fox News why Vance was pulled out of the Iran talks. He said the vice president was doing a “very good job” but immediately mentioned Vance’s post (he wasn’t asked about it).

 

“He basically just left one thing out,” Trump said. “ ‘If we had it to do again, would you do it again?’ And the answer is ‘absolutely yes.’ ”

 

The dynamic between Trump and Vance will be very closely studied. Will Trump back him if Vance runs in 2028? The answer, as of now, doesn’t appear to be “definitely.”

 

In an October interview with Mark Halperin, Vance said he thought Trump would endorse him if he ran for president. Trump was asked about this and said the two had never discussed the matter. He declined to say if he’d support him over others.

 

This is an edition of the Politics newsletter, bringing you an expert guide to what’s driving D.C. every day. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

People and Policies I’m Watching

 

Sean Cairncross: The national cyber director is leaving his role coordinating cybersecurity policy as the White House responds to a wave of cyber threats posed by what is believed to be new AI models.

 

Rob Bonta: California’s attorney general has issued an investigative subpoena to Nvidia, opening a probe into the conduct of the chip maker.

 

Trump’s Friday: The president has a policy meeting this morning and will hold a news conference at 12 p.m. ET. He will then host a reception at 3:30 p.m.

What I’m Following

 
 
J. SCOTT APPLEWHITE/AP
 

Republicans are more willing to block Trump’s nominees. A series of Trump picks have run into trouble in the past week, with a Government Accountability Office nominee getting some tough questions on Thursday after the FDA selection was pulled days ago. It shows that Republicans in this lame duck Congress are less willing to hold their noses and back nominees as they head into the minority.

 

The Pentagon is struggling to shore up GOP support for a record-setting budget. The effort to push through a $1.5 trillion spending request has stalled, as several GOP members balked at the idea of passing $350 billion of it through reconciliation. The uncertainty comes as the government barrels toward a Dec. 11 deadline, after which funding for the federal government will lapse.

 

The U.S. has floated the idea of NATO membership for Ukraine in recent talks. In closed-door peace talks over the past few months, Trump’s son-in-law and special envoy Jared Kushner has discussed an idea once believed to be dead-on-arrival: NATO membership for Ukraine if it cedes territory to Russia. A U.S. official said negotiators are discussing many ideas, but both Ukraine and Russia would need to agree to any final deal.

 
 
 

What Else Is Happening

 

• The Senate passed a bipartisan bill designed to speed up energy, mining and other infrastructure projects, overcoming concerns by many Democrats that it would weaken environmental protection laws.

 

• The Federal Reserve board approved a smaller budget for pay increases at its 12 regional banks, with employees at the banks being told to expect 1% annual raises, down from 3% this year.

 

• Russian President Vladimir Putin scored a significant public relations coup in China this week, five years after launching an invasion of Ukraine that cast him as an pariah.

 

• New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani signed a horse-drawn carriage ban into law, ending a Central Park fixture that has been around for more than 160 years.
